corpus_definition: a small specific part or feature of something larger

forms.definition: one small fact or part of something bigger
forms.example: He told me every tiny detail of the story.

syn.note: Formal; often plural: 'Please send me the particulars of the job.'
Related: one idea or fact in a talk or text; not always small.
Related: an important or typical part of something, like a feature of a building.
Related: something true; a detail is a small fact inside a bigger story.
Related: one basic part of something; more formal.

forms.definition: to give all the small facts about something, one by one
forms.example: The report details the cost of every new school.

syn.note: Related: to say what something is like; you may not give every small fact.
Related: to write things one after another, often without explaining them.
Formal: to say exactly what is needed or planned.
To write each thing on a list separately, like on a bill. British spelling: itemise.

forms.definition: having many small facts or parts, with nothing left out
forms.example: She gave us a detailed map of the old city of Bukhara.

syn.note: Careful and complete; often about work or a check.
Formal: covering everything about a subject.
Related, easy word: 'a full report' has all the information.
Related: about the person doing the work, not the result.

ant.note: Only the main ideas, not exact: 'a rough plan'.
About the whole thing, without small facts: 'a general idea'.

forms.note: No adverb in this family. Learners say 'in detail': 'She explained it in detail.'

context.text: My grandmother remembers every detail of her wedding in Samarkand. She gave me a detailed description of the food, the music and the guests.

reviewer_note: 'Detailed' is a participle adjective; -ed is not in the affix table, so no affix is claimed. No real adverb (use 'in detail').

corpus_definition: A very bad spirit that causes evil in many stories.

forms.definition: an evil spirit in stories and religions that makes people do bad things
forms.example: He told a story about a trickster devil.
forms.note: With 'the' and often a capital letter, it means the most powerful evil spirit in Christianity and Islam.

syn.note: Very close; an evil spirit, often in films and stories.
Old-fashioned or literary word for an evil spirit.
Related: a frightening creature, but not always a spirit.

ant.note: A good spirit that helps people; the opposite of a devil.

forms.definition: to cook food with hot spices such as mustard or pepper
forms.example: The cook devilled the chicken legs with mustard and chilli.
forms.note: Belongs to devil = hot, spicy cooking (deviled eggs), not the evil spirit. Rare; American spelling deviled.

forms.definition: very bad or wicked, like an evil spirit
forms.example: The villain in the film had a devilish laugh.
forms.note: It can also mean playful in a slightly naughty way: 'a devilish smile'.

syn.note: Very bad and cruel; common in fairy tales.
Easy word; very bad and harmful.
Cruel and clever in a bad way; also 'very difficult': a fiendish puzzle.
Related: only a little bad, like a child who does not obey.

ant.note: Very good, kind or beautiful, like an angel.

forms.definition: extremely; very much
forms.example: The last question in the test was devilishly hard.
forms.note: Belongs to devil used as a strong word meaning 'very', not evil spirits. A little old-fashioned and informal.

context.text: In old Uzbek stories, a devil sometimes tricks travellers on the road at night. My grandfather told these tales with a devilish smile, and we were always scared.

reviewer_note: Verb 'devil' (spicy cooking) and adverb 'devilishly' (= very) shown as other_meaning so no real word is hidden.

corpus_definition: A drawing that explains how something works.

forms.definition: a simple drawing that shows how something works or is built
forms.example: Look at the diagram to fix the machine.

syn.note: A drawing or table that shows information, often numbers.
Related, easy word: any picture made with a pen or pencil.
Related: a drawing of a building or machine from above.
Related: a quick drawing without many details.
Related: a drawing with lines that shows numbers changing.

forms.definition: to show or explain something with a simple drawing
forms.example: The teacher diagrammed the parts of a flower on the board.
forms.note: British spelling: diagrammed, diagramming (double m in both British and American English).

syn.note: To show information in a drawing or table.
Related, easy word: to make any picture.
Related: to draw quickly and simply.

forms.definition: shown as a simple drawing that explains something
forms.example: The book gives a diagrammatic view of the human heart.

syn.note: Formal and technical; showing only the main parts.
Related: connected with pictures and drawings.

forms.definition: by using a simple drawing that explains something
forms.example: The water cycle is shown diagrammatically on page 12.

syn.note: Technical; showing only the main parts.
Related: using pictures, charts or drawings.

context.text: Our science teacher drew a diagram of the heart on the board. The textbook shows the same idea in a diagrammatic way, with red and blue arrows for the blood.

reviewer_note: No affix claimed: diagrammatic = diagram + -atic, and removing -ic leaves no real word.

corpus_definition: to turn a control to select a number or setting; a round control panel

forms.definition: a round part with numbers that you turn or read, on a phone, clock or machine
forms.example: Turn the dial on the oven to 180 degrees.

syn.note: Related: a small round handle you turn; it may have no numbers.
Related: any button or switch that makes a machine work.
Related: you press or flip a switch to turn something on or off.

forms.definition: to press or turn the numbers on a phone, or turn a control to a setting
forms.example: She dialed the number and waited for an answer.
forms.note: British spelling: dialled, dialling. American: dialed, dialing.

syn.note: Related, easy word: you dial a number to call someone.
Related: to speak to someone by phone.
Related: British English for 'phone someone'.
Related: to turn a radio to a station.

forms.note: No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandmother still has an old phone with a round dial. She dials her sister's number slowly, one number at a time, and waits for her to answer.

reviewer_note: One row joins the verb and the noun of the same meaning (conversion), so one map. Only one spelling exists, so context uses noun and verb of 'dial'.

corpus_definition: Using computer technology to store or show information as numbers.

forms.definition: the process of changing books, pictures or sound into a form a computer can use
forms.example: The digitization of old library books takes many years.
forms.note: British spelling: digitisation.

syn.note: Related: starting to use computers for a job. British spelling: computerisation.
Related: copying paper pages into a computer with a machine.

forms.definition: any one of the numbers from 0 to 9
forms.example: My phone number has nine digits.
forms.note: Belongs to the old root meaning 'a single number' (also 'a finger'), not computer technology. 'Digital' first meant 'using numbers'.

forms.definition: to change pictures, text or sound into a form a computer can use
forms.example: The museum is digitizing its old photos.
forms.note: British spelling: digitise.

syn.note: Related: to copy a paper page into a computer with a machine.
Related: to start using computers for a job. British spelling: computerise.

forms.definition: using computers to keep or show information as numbers
forms.example: I prefer reading digital books instead of paper ones.

syn.note: Using electricity and computer chips; very close in everyday use.
Related: connected to the internet; digital things are not always online.
Related: made by a computer and not real, like a virtual tour.

ant.note: Using moving parts or waves, not numbers: an analog watch has hands. British spelling: analogue.

forms.definition: by using computer technology
forms.example: All the photos are stored digitally on my phone.

syn.note: Using computers or electronic machines: 'pay electronically'.

context.text: My father digitized all our old family photos last year. Now we keep them in a digital album and share them digitally with our relatives in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: Root 'digit' (a single number) shown as noun other_meaning; digitization is the noun for this meaning.

forms.definition: the state of having very little light
forms.example: In the dimness of the room, I could not see her face.

syn.note: Easy word; darkness can mean no light at all.
Low light that often feels sad; a little literary.
Related: a dark area where light is blocked.

forms.definition: to make a light less bright, or to become less bright
forms.example: Please dim the lights before the film starts.

syn.note: To make or become darker; not only about lamps.
Related: 'lower the lights' is a common, easy way to say it.
Related: to become weaker slowly, like a colour or a sound.

forms.definition: not giving or having much light, so things are hard to see
forms.example: The light in the room was very dim.
forms.note: In informal English it can also mean 'not clever': 'He's a bit dim.'

syn.note: Weak and hard to see or hear: 'a faint light'.
Not bright or shiny: 'a dull grey sky'.
Related, easy word: dark can mean no light at all; dim means a little light.
Related: 'a weak light' is not strong.
Related: dark in a way that feels sad.

forms.definition: with only a little light, or not clearly
forms.example: The old teahouse was dimly lit by candles.
forms.note: Also used about memory: 'I dimly remember my first school.'

syn.note: In a weak way that is hard to see or hear.
Related: not clearly, often about memory.

ant.note: With a lot of strong light.

people.definition: a switch that makes a lamp brighter or less bright
people.example: We put a dimmer in the bedroom so the light can be soft at night.

context.text: The lights in the theatre dimmed slowly before the concert. In the dim hall, I could only see the stage, which was brightly lit.

reviewer_note: Informal 'dim = not clever' only mentioned in a note. 'Dimmer' is the device (-er thing), not the comparative.

corpus_definition: To put something into a liquid for a short time.

forms.definition: a thick cold sauce that you put bread or vegetables into
forms.example: We had fresh carrots with a garlic yogurt dip.
forms.note: Other meanings of the noun: a quick swim ('a dip in the lake') and a small fall ('a dip in prices').

syn.note: Easy word; a sauce is often hot and poured on food, a dip is thick and cold.
Related: soft food you put on bread with a knife.

forms.definition: to put something into a liquid quickly and then take it out
forms.example: She likes to dip bread into olive oil.

syn.note: Informal; very common with biscuits or bread in tea.
Formal: to put something completely under a liquid.
Related: you leave something in liquid for a long time.
Related: to push something into liquid suddenly and with force.

forms.note: No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: My little brother likes to dip his bread into hot tea. At the party, we also had fresh vegetables with a garlic yogurt dip.

reviewer_note: Only one spelling in the family; the noun 'dip' (sauce) is shown as the same-meaning conversion. 'Dipper' (ladle) left out as rare.

corpus_definition: Having a physical or mental condition that limits movement or learning.

forms.definition: a condition of the body or mind that makes some everyday activities hard
forms.example: The school helps students with a disability to take part in every lesson.

syn.note: Formal or medical; often about one sense: 'hearing impairment'.
Old-fashioned and now often thought rude; use disability.
Related: a health problem that lasts a long time.

forms.definition: to hurt someone so their body or mind cannot work in the usual way
forms.example: The car accident disabled him for life.
forms.note: It also means 'to stop a machine or system working': 'disable the alarm'.

syn.note: Related: to hurt someone; the harm may not last.
Very strong; about people it can sound rude today.
Related: to make someone unable to move part of the body. British spelling: paralyse.

forms.definition: having a condition of the body or mind that limits movement or learning
forms.example: The building has easy access for disabled people.
forms.note: Say 'disabled people' or 'people with disabilities'. 'Handicapped' is old-fashioned.

syn.note: Old-fashioned and now often thought rude; use disabled.
Related, formal: about one part, e.g. 'visually impaired' = cannot see well.

ant.note: Having no physical condition that limits movement.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

context.text: My cousin has been disabled since a car accident, but he still works as a teacher. His school has ramps, so his disability does not stop him from getting to class.

reviewer_note: Headword is the participle adjective (relation participial). dis- claimed only on disability (= lack of ability); disable is not a clean opposite of able. Polite-language notes added.

corpus_definition: A conversation where people share their opinions on a topic.

forms.definition: a talk where people share their ideas and opinions about something
forms.example: We had a long discussion about the future plan.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word: 'We had a talk about it.'
Any talk between people; a discussion usually has a topic.
More formal; people often have opposite opinions.
Related: formal talk between groups to solve a problem. American spelling also dialog.
Related: a friendly, informal talk, often not serious.

forms.definition: to talk about something with other people and share ideas
forms.example: We discussed the plan over dinner.
forms.note: No 'about' after it: say 'discuss the plan', not 'discuss about the plan'.

syn.note: Easy, everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Informal phrasal verb, often before a decision: 'Let's talk it over.'
More formal; people often disagree.
Related: to think carefully; you can do it alone.

forms.note: No common adjective. 'Discussable' exists but is very rare.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: Our class had a long discussion about the new bus route. We discussed the problem for an hour and then wrote a letter to the city council.

reviewer_note: Trap for Uzbek/Russian speakers: 'discuss about' is wrong; noted on the verb.

corpus_definition: To put something where people can see it.

forms.definition: a group of things arranged for people to look at
forms.example: The shop has a beautiful window display of silk scarves.
forms.note: It also means the screen of a phone or computer: 'a bright display'.

syn.note: A bigger public show, often in a museum or gallery.
Easy word: 'a flower show'.
One object or a small group of objects in a museum.
Related: the way something is shown, or a talk with pictures.

forms.definition: to put something in a place where people can see it
forms.example: The museum will display rare paintings.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
More formal; used for museums and galleries.
To show the best qualities of something.
Related: to show or give something formally.

ant.note: To put something where people cannot see it.

forms.note: No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: The museum in Samarkand will display old coins next month. The display will also include pottery and silk from the Silk Road.

reviewer_note: dis- is not a real prefix here (play is not the opposite); no affix claimed. Screen meaning only in a note (same spelling).
